annotation_description: Fetching a basic Island instead of Watery Grave means the player won't have access to black mana on turn 2. With Psychic Frog (UB) in hand as one of the best early plays available, having black mana is important. The player already has an untapped land from turn 1 (likely producing blue), and getting Watery Grave untapped (paying 2 life) would enable casting Psychic Frog this turn. A basic Island only provides blue mana, which they likely already have.

Evoking or casting Solitude when the opponent has no creatures on the battlefield wastes a premium removal spell for no value. Meanwhile, the player desperately needs to develop mana - they only have 1 Island in play with expensive cards in hand (Psychic Frog, Quantum Riddler, etc). Missing the land drop by not playing Flooded Strand sets them further behind on mana development.

annotation_description: The player evoked Solitude by exiling Atraxa, Grand Unifier — one of the most powerful cards in their hand — to remove an unknown target (likely nothing threatening on board since the opponent has no visible creatures). Atraxa is an extremely high-value card being pitched for minimal gain. Furthermore, Solitude's ETB exiles 'up to one other target creature,' but the opponent appears to have no creatures on the battlefield, making this evoke accomplish almost nothing while sacrificing a premium card. Even if there were a target, exiling Atraxa (a 7-mana bomb) to evoke Solitude on turn 3 when the opponent has no board presence is a terrible trade.

annotation_description: Disrupting Shoal with alternative cost requires exiling a blue card with mana value equal to X, and X must match the target spell's mana value (5 for Solitude). The highest MV blue card in hand is Flare of Denial at MV 3, so X=3 cannot counter Solitude (MV 5). This wastes both Disrupting Shoal AND the exiled blue card (likely Flare of Denial, their best remaining counterspell) for absolutely nothing.

With Psychic Frog (UB) and Quantum Riddler (3UU) in hand, plus two Force of Negations that need blue cards to exile, the player needs both blue and black mana. They already have an Island on the battlefield. Fetching a basic Plains provides white mana but doesn't help cast anything in their hand. Fetching Watery Grave (paying 2 life) would give access to black mana for Psychic Frog on turn 3, which is the most important early play. Alternatively, Hallowed Fountain could provide blue+white, but white isn't needed for anything in hand. The basic Plains is essentially a dead mana source since nothing in hand requires white mana, while black mana is critically needed for Psychic Frog.

Discarded Force of Negation to pump Psychic Frog when Griselbrand is an uncastable 8-mana creature with no reanimation support. Force of Negation is a live spell that can be cast for free on the opponent's turn by exiling the remaining blue card (the other Force of Negation). Griselbrand provides zero value in hand with only 3 lands and no way to cheat it into play.

Discarding Force of Negation to pump Psychic Frog removes a key counterspell from hand. With only 3 cards in hand (Force of Negation, Griselbrand, Solitude), Force of Negation is the most flexible defensive card - it can counter noncreature spells for free on the opponent's turn. The opponent has no board presence yet, so the Frog is already likely to connect. Discarding Griselbrand (which is nearly uncastable at 8 mana with only 3 lands and no reanimation visible) would preserve the counterspell while still pumping the Frog. Griselbrand in the graveyard could even fuel Psychic Frog's flying ability later.

Discarding Griselbrand to pump Psychic Frog wastes one of the most powerful cards in the deck. With Watery Grave providing black mana, Griselbrand could potentially be a reanimation target or hard-cast threat later. Solitude, on the other hand, has already been used (two copies in graveyard) and while it provides removal via Evoke, discarding it to pump the Frog is more reasonable since it's a white card in a deck that seems to want blue/black resources. Griselbrand in the graveyard is only useful if there's a reanimation package, but even then, keeping it in hand preserves optionality. Solitude as a discard is better because it's less impactful as a card in hand when you only have 3 lands and no white card to pitch for evoke anyway (you'd need another white card which you don't have).

Discarding Solitude during the beginning of turn 4 (before combat) to pump Psychic Frog with a +1/+1 counter. Solitude is an extremely powerful card that can be evoked to exile a creature by pitching a white card, and it serves as the only remaining card in hand. While pumping the Frog is valuable, discarding the last card in hand means GPT4om Vorthos is now hellbent with no interaction available. However, with all three lands tapped and Solitude requiring a white card to evoke (and no other white cards in hand), the Solitude was effectively dead for its evoke mode. The question is whether holding it for a future hard-cast (at 5 mana) or as a potential evoke target later (if a white card is drawn) would be more valuable than the +1/+1 counter now. Given the opponent has an empty board and no cards visible, the aggressive pump to make Frog a 2/3 (or 3/4 with prior counters) for combat damage + card draw is reasonable, but going hellbent sacrifices future flexibility.

Exiling Griselbrand from the graveyard to give Psychic Frog flying is wasteful. Griselbrand is a powerful reanimation target that could potentially be brought back later. The graveyard contains less valuable cards like Polluted Delta, Flooded Strand, and Solitude that would be better exile fodder since they have little utility in the graveyard.

Casting Ephemerate targeting Psychic Frog is suboptimal since Psychic Frog has no enter-the-battlefield ability. The flicker accomplishes nothing meaningful. Discarding Ephemerate to Psychic Frog's pump ability would give a +1/+1 counter, making it a bigger attacker that draws a card on combat damage.

Casting Faithful Mending in precombat main when Psychic Frog would connect unblocked (opponent has no creatures). Attacking first draws a card from Frog's combat damage trigger, giving more cards and better information for Faithful Mending's draw-then-discard.

Exiled Faithful Mending (which has flashback {1}{W}{U}) from the graveyard to give Psychic Frog flying, just to deal 1 damage. With 0 cards in hand, Faithful Mending's flashback would draw 2 cards and gain 2 life next turn, which is far more valuable than 1 point of flying damage against a 20-life opponent.

Llama4 Stoic discarded Whir of Invention, which is their best way to find and deploy Goblin Charbelcher at instant speed (and can use artifacts to help pay via Improvise). With no lands in play, the Charbelcher combo is their primary win condition, and Whir of Invention is the most powerful enabler to tutor for it at instant speed. Meanwhile, they have three copies of Thundertrap Trainer which are relatively low-impact creatures, and one of those would have been a much better discard choice.

Llama4 Stoic is discarding to hand size and chose to discard Goblin Charbelcher. While they have two copies, Charbelcher is their primary win condition in what appears to be a combo deck (with two Lotus Blooms suspended). Discarding a redundant Thundertrap Trainer would preserve both combo pieces. The Thundertrap Trainers are card selection creatures but with three copies in hand, one is easily expendable. Keeping both Charbelchers provides insurance against discard effects or if one gets countered.

Chose to exile Ephemerate (a useful rebound spell) instead of Undercity Sewers (a tapped land with no graveyard utility) as the third card for Psychic Frog's flying activation. Ephemerate has potential future value if a creature with ETB is drawn, while the tapped land is essentially worthless in the graveyard.

Goblin Charbelcher is Llama4 Stoic's primary win condition in what appears to be a Charbelcher combo deck. The deck likely runs few or no lands, making Charbelcher potentially lethal when activated. Discarding the only copy in hand (with one already in the graveyard) removes the main path to winning the game. While they have Tameshi, Reality Architect which could potentially return an artifact from the graveyard, that's a fragile multi-step plan requiring specific board conditions.

Casting Faithful Mending during their own precombat main phase instead of waiting for the opponent's end step. With Psychic Frog already tapped and no other cards in hand, there's no benefit to casting it now. Waiting until the opponent's end step would keep all 4 mana open during the opponent's turn for any drawn interaction (counterspells, removal, etc.), and the drawn cards would still be available for the next turn.

Spell Snare is highly relevant in this matchup as it cleanly counters Psychic Frog (MV 2), the opponent's primary threat. Meanwhile, having three Thundertrap Trainers is redundant - casting all three is unlikely and they're just 1/2 bodies that dig for spells.

Used Force of Negation instead of Disrupting Shoal to counter Teferi, Time Raveler (MV 3). Disrupting Shoal could counter it by exiling Tameshi, Reality Architect (a blue card with MV 3) from hand. Force of Negation is a more versatile and powerful counterspell that should be saved for future threats, especially since it can counter noncreature spells for free on the opponent's turn. Additionally, Force of Negation on your own turn may require hard-casting for {1}{U}{U} which is mana-intensive.
